item.title: What Protections Exist for Binance’s Customers?
item.description:
The staggering digital hack at Binance, where criminals made off with $6.3 billion in digital coins in a breach that the company revealed on Thursday, is a reminder that putting money into cryptocurrency still involves a fair bit of risk.

Binance has said it will reimburse customers who have experienced losses. It has no real choice but to make people whole, lest its customers’ confidence sink even further than it already has in the wake of such a large attack.

But there does not appear to be any U.S. governmental or regulatory entity that could force Binance or other troubled crypto companies to help customers. And minimal regulation is exactly what early crypto enthusiasts wanted, even as the Biden administration tried to rein in the industry before the Trump administration undid much of its work.

Here are some questions and answers about the incident and its implications.

The hack affected the original Binance (Binance.com), which the company blocks U.S. customers from using (though some probably do so anyway via virtual private networks). There is also a small Binance.Us platform for U.S. users in certain states, which was not part of the hack.

In an announcement on its website, the company said it would “cover all losses” using its own funds and its “secure asset fund for users.” The SAFU is an emergency fund that Binance set up on its own. “It is designed to reduce the potential impact on users if an extreme event does happen,” according to the company.

The fund had $1 billion in Bitcoin as of 2026, according to the website. The price of Bitcoin has fallen about 30 percent this year, though the company says it replenishes the fund if it falls below $800 million in value.

“User funds are safe,” it added in its announcement. The company has suspended withdrawals for now. “Thank you for your support!” the company said at the conclusion of its update.

Not many, though plenty of customers believe otherwise, since there has been automatic deposit insurance at banks for decades.

If the company that holds your cryptocurrency, or provides storage for your digital wallet, is hacked or goes out of business, there are no federal guarantees or rules to help, according to the Federal Trade Commission.

This is unlikely to change any time soon. In a podcast interview this year, Mike Selig, the chair of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, called for the “minimum effective dose of regulation,” lest it “strangle” industries or be “paternalistic.”

And even if there were robust regulations, it would be hard to enforce them against companies that are not in the United States.

They highlight the elevated risks of holding digital assets and underscore that government protections do not apply to crypto.

“The nature of virtual currency may lead to an increased risk of fraud or cyberattack,” Robinhood said in its 37-page agreement. “Any bond or trust account maintained by Robinhood Crypto for the benefit of its customers may not be sufficient to cover all losses incurred by customers.”

A spokesman for Robinhood said most of its assets were in cold storage, which means access keys are held off the internet.Fidelity, Coinbase and other brokerages echo that warning. Coinbase also notes that its crime insurance coverage for systemwide cyberattacks does not extend to losses that occur because of a breach or loss of credentials.

“It is your responsibility to use a strong password and maintain control of all login credentials you use to access Coinbase,” it said on its website. Be sure to read all of the fine print.

When a bank or brokerage firm gets into trouble, there are two major — but different — entities that offer guarantees.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which is backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, provides depositors with coverage up to certain limits when an insured bank fails.

The Securities Investor Protection Corporation, known as SIPC, serves as a backstop for brokerage firms when, for example, one shuts down while it still has active customers with holdings. It’s a nonprofit corporation that was created under the Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970.

SIPC generally covers up to $500,000 of securities, like stocks and bonds, and cash (including a $250,000 limit for the cash component) for each customer. It can be higher for people with multiple accounts.

Even then, according to the SIPC website, it does not protect any digital or crypto asset unless it is deemed a “security.” That generally means it is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The F.D.I.C. and SIPC coverage do not protect against losses due to theft or fraud, which are covered by other rules — and those laws hinge on how the theft or fraud occurred. (SIPC does, however, step in if a failed brokerage firm was in on the thievery.)

It’s never wise to bet on a government bailout. But it’s also a reasonable question. The C.F.T.C. says on its website that the federal government has no obligation to help, but that doesn’t mean a friendly regulator or politicians wouldn’t do so anyway.

Mr. Trump’s family has a large stake in the crypto industry, and his own net worth has grown substantially because of his exposure. A collapse in prices or confidence in companies powering the industry would affect him directly.

In 2023, Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, pleaded guilty to money-laundering violations and eventually spent four months in federal prison. The company also pleaded guilty and agreed to pay $4.3 billion in fines and restitution.

The White House referred a request for comment on the possibility of company or industry bailouts to the Department of Justice, which emailed a statement.

“Binance remains under an obligation to cooperate with law enforcement pursuant to its plea agreement,” it said. “The department remains committed to combating cybercrime, protecting victims and holding accountable those who exploit digital technologies to commit financial crimes.”

Regulators and prosecutors had accused Mr. Zhao and the company of allowing terrorists to use the platform. Last year, Mr. Trump pardoned him.

item.title: How The New York Times Is Covering the Midterm Elections
item.description:
Much has changed in the nearly 20 years that Patricia Mazzei, a political correspondent for The New York Times, has covered elections. But one aspect of her life has remained the same: hitting the road.

Ms. Mazzei has driven more than 1,525 miles through Florida, Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina this year while reporting on midterm races for The Times’s Politics desk.

“I try to get as wide a variety of reporting experiences as I can,” said Ms. Mazzei, who covered elections at The Miami Herald for a decade before arriving at The Times in 2017. “It’s incredible to get to explore different parts of the country.”

From her home base in Florida, Ms. Mazzei is among more than 400 Times reporters, editors, data analysts, video journalists and photographers who have been covering the thousands of races for House and Senate seats, governorships, judgeships and more throughout the United States.

Over days that can stretch from 3 a.m. wake-up calls to whenever a campaign rally ends at night, they have sought to nail down candidates’ positions; scrutinized polling data to spot trends; and spent countless hours talking with political advisers, pollsters, organizing groups and voters.

“It’s a big country and voters are complicated — and sometimes contradictory — and we always have plenty to explain on and after election night about what happened and how,” Ms. Mazzei said.

This year, The Times will have more than 100 reporters in at least 30 states on election night. The goal, said Michael Cooper, The Times’s Politics editor, is to take readers inside interesting races with national implications.

“This election will not only tell us who controls Congress and give us clues about what the last two years of President Trump’s term might look like, but will tell us a great deal about the nation itself,” he said. “What issues motivate Americans, and what do they want from their government? And how are both parties and candidates evolving in a time of rapid change?”

A growing part of that mission is visual, including on-the-ground photography and video.

The Times will have three video teams in the battleground states of Maine, Michigan and Texas talking with voters at the polls on election night. They will be part of a group of more than 40 people overall who will be involved in video coverage across a 24-hour operation run from newsrooms in London, New York, Los Angeles and Seoul.

The aim, said Beckey Bright, The Times’s manager of video editorial operations, is to provide a snapshot of voter sentiment, the candidates they support and the issues that matter to them.

For the first time, two journalists on the Visual Investigations team will also monitor the news to help assess questions about videos and images that may have been generated by artificial intelligence, said Mark Scheffler, the editor who leads the desk.

A major thrust of The Times’s reporting also happens behind the scenes, as more than 100 data journalists crunch the election results back at the New York newsroom. They are looking to illustrate trends for readers in specific races, said Benjamin Hoffman, a deputy editor on The Times’s election analytics team.

“We want to explain concepts like polling error with hard data in a way that hopefully takes out some of the uneasiness people have when looking at things like polls,” he said.

The team’s work is human-powered — not driven by A.I.

“One of our principles is that data and estimates should be checked, interpreted and analyzed by humans,” said Lindsey Rogers Cook, a deputy editor for election analytics.

On election night, The Times will rely on data from The Associated Press to regularly update results from more than 6,000 races. Those initial returns, along with precinct-level voting results from more than 100 web scrapers, will also feed the Needle, The Times’s estimate for final results.

New this year will be a feature called Times Voter Trends, which will publish the day after the election and break down estimates for the results of House and Senate elections by age, race, education and gender in every state. The goal is to reveal how different groups voted and identify shifts from previous elections.

Part of the fun, Ms. Mazzei said, is that voters cannot be reduced to a category on a spreadsheet.

“Voters don’t fit in neat partisan boxes and make decisions often based on their personal histories or emotions,” she said.

Some races, like the Senate battleground contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Ohio and Texas that are expected to determine the balance of power, are priorities. But more often than not, Times reporters flag interesting and potentially pivotal contests worthy of more attention.

“They’re the ones out in the field talking to candidates, voters, sources, matching what they’re hearing with what they’re seeing to divine the impact of redistricting, broader political and societal trends, and demographic shifts,” said Ben Shpigel, an editor helping to oversee live political coverage.

Ultimately, he said, the goal is not only to help readers understand the stakes of an election that will determine how much power President Trump will have for the rest of his term, but also why they’re seeing the results they are, both locally and nationally.

“On Nov. 3,” he said, “I want readers to feel like the scope and totality of our coverage prepared them for any and all outcomes.”

item.title: William Nordhaus Has Died. Nobelist Influenced Climate Policy.
item.description:
William D. Nordhaus, a Yale economist and Nobel laureate who tabulated the economic wreckage of carbon emissions and influenced climate policy across several presidential administrations, died on Friday at his home in New Haven. He was 85.

The cause was glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer, according to a statement from Yale University.

In 2018, Professor Nordhaus shared the Nobel in economic science with Paul M. Romer, an economist at New York University. The Nobel committee cited Professor Nordhaus’s work in developing a method to balance climate change’s long-term damage with the costs required to contain it.

The model, which Professor Nordhaus refined over decades, has underpinned dozens of regulations around the world aimed at limiting fossil fuels and seeded the ground for a new field of research that bridges the gap between economics and earth science.

“He played a crucial role in terms of bringing consideration of the natural environment into the mainstream of economics, whereas earlier, it was sort of a fringe area,” said Robert Stavins, director of the environmental economics program at Harvard, who wrote about Professor Nordhaus’s impact.

Professor Nordhaus saw climate change as a clear threat to humankind, but he emphasized that potential damages must be balanced with the economic cost of preventing them. “Climate stabilization would appear enormously expensive,” he concluded, in his initial paper describing the model.

To deal with the problem efficiently, Professor Nordhaus proposed a modest carbon tax that would escalate over time. The idea gained support in the 2000s among liberals like Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, and Republicans such as former secretaries of state James A. Baker III and George P. Shultz, who championed it as a “conservative climate solution.”Ultimately, although carbon taxes have proven politically toxic in the face of corporate opposition and have only rarely been instituted, many countries and sub-national governments like states and provinces have set up emissions-trading systems that impose carbon limits and use markets to set prices. One such proposal passed the U.S. House of Representatives in 2009 but died in the Senate.

Perhaps a more enduring outgrowth of Professor Nordhaus’s model is a metric called the “social cost of carbon,” which quantifies the benefits of combating climate change. In the Obama administration, it became a fundamental tool for regulating emissions from power plants and vehicles, until the second Trump administration banned its use in rule making last year.

The Nobel was widely seen as a rebuke to the Trump administration, which had at the time begun to dismantle the building blocks of American environmental policy; Mr. Trump often called climate change a “hoax.”

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

Although colleagues found Professor Nordhaus to be scrupulously apolitical, he gave an interview to the Nobel committee in 2018 in which he decried what he called Mr. Trump’s “ludicrous statements about climate change.”

Winning the prize, he said, “gives a kind of courage and heart to the people who are on the right side of history.”

William Dawbney Nordhaus, the third of four children, was born in Albuquerque on May 31, 1941. His father, Robert J. Nordhaus, was a Yale-educated lawyer for American Indian rights; he also was an outdoorsman who started a ski resort in the nearby Sandia Mountains and helped build a popular tram to bring visitors to the tourist destination. His mother, Virginia (Riggs) Nordhaus, oversaw the home.

Professor Nordhaus graduated in 1959 from Phillips Academy in Andover, Mass., and in 1963 received a bachelor’s degree in economics from Yale University.

In 1967, he completed his doctoral studies in economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, studying under future Nobelists Robert M. Solow, Kenneth Arrow and Paul A. Samuelson, with whom Professor Nordhaus continually updated and later took over primary authorship of a widely used textbook, “Economics.”

He returned to Yale in 1967 as an assistant professor just as the environmental movement was gaining steam. He became interested in accounting for planetary harms after reading an article in a Trans World Airlines in-flight magazine that criticized the traditional measure of economic output, the gross national product.

“In the words of a young radical, don’t tell me about your GNP. To me, it’s really Gross National Pollution,” Professor Nordhaus recalled that it said. “I thought, ‘Wow, that’s really cute. But is it true?’”

That question launched an effort to quantify the impact of natural resource depletion. The work to reflect the environment in national economic statistics took another step forward in a National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine report that Professor Nordhaus led in 1999 and continues today, as governments have tried to supplement official metrics that ignore many aspects of human welfare.

In the 1970s, awareness of the impact of carbon dioxide on the earth’s climate was just dawning. Professor Nordhaus hit upon the problem in 1974 during a residency at the International Institute of Applied Systems Analysis in Vienna where he shared an office with a climatologist who encouraged him to study linkages with the economy. That led to the first known paper integrating carbon emissions into an economic model that estimated what it might cost to limit the fallout for the climate.

Soon after his return to the United States, Mr. Nordhaus went to Washington, D.C., to serve as a member of President Jimmy Carter’s Council of Economic Advisers. In close communication with his brother Robert, an energy lawyer who wrote key provisions of the Clean Air Act of 1970 and later was general counsel at the Department of Energy under President Bill Clinton, he generated recommendations about how to gauge the economic costs and benefits of proposed regulations. The concept was legally mandated for federal rule-making processes in 1981, although the criteria have changed with the priorities of successive administrations.

Back at Yale, Professor Nordhaus kept working to quantify the implications of climate change for economic growth. It was a lonely project: Few others were studying the question, and when he finished a model that assessed the cost of several approaches to limiting emissions, mainstream economics journals rejected the submission.

“They didn’t see why this was important. That’s why it was published in Science,” Lint Barrage, an associate professor of energy and climate economics at ETH Zurich, a public research university, who studied under Mr. Nordhaus and worked with him on later updates to the model, said in an interview. “You don’t stick with that topic and swim against the stream if it’s not something you’re really convinced about.”

As Professor Nordhaus’ research gained mainstream acceptance, it also came under fire. One challenge arrived in the form of a 2006 report commissioned by the British government that called for a much more aggressive approach to limiting carbon emissions than Professor Nordhaus had recommended.

The core dispute was over how much policymakers should value the welfare of future generations compared with that of people now. Professor Nordhaus wrote a withering riposte, and the question remains central to debates over how much to pay for climate mitigation.

Another disagreement arose over whether conventional economic analysis could be applied when considering the potentially infinite costs of unlikely but catastrophic climate disasters. This one came from the Harvard economics professor Martin Weitzman, to whom Professor Nordhaus respectfully responded that such scenarios were limited. He would later call Professor Weitzman, who died by suicide in 2019, the “pre-eminent environmental economist of the modern era.”

Other criticisms arose over whether the harms from climate change should be balanced with conventional metrics of economic growth, which many see as the wrong yardstick.

“When he carried out that analysis, his view was, ‘Let the chips fall where they may,’” said Professor Stavins. “As a result, the policy actions and trajectories that he was recommending early on were not as ambitious as many advocates would like.”

Under the Biden administration, federal climate policy largely abandoned the idea of pricing carbon, favoring subsidies as both more politically palatable and potentially more equitable in shifting behavior. And over time, Professor Nordhaus adjusted his model to incorporate new science, pushing up his estimate of the appropriate carbon price significantly. Other economists have now constructed their own integrated models that reach different conclusions.

In 1964, he married Barbara Feise, who later became a psychoanalyst. In addition to his wife, he is survived by three children, Jeff, Monica and Rebecca; a brother, Richard; a sister, Elizabeth; and three granddaughters.

Another legacy of Professor Nordhaus’s work may only now be taking root.

As international climate diplomacy floundered in recent years, he proposed the concept of a “climate club” of willing nations that would impose trade penalties on nonparticipants. One such effort took effect this year: the European Union’s carbon border adjustment mechanism, which levies tariffs on goods from outside the bloc that correspond with their impact on the climate.

item.title: Aramco Profit Jumps Despite Damaging Attacks on Pipelines and Refineries
item.description:
For Saudi Aramco, the war in Iran has brought extraordinary disruptions to its exports and damaging direct attacks on its facilities. But that has not dented the company’s bottom line.

The state-owned oil giant reported on Tuesday an adjusted net income of $31.2 billion between July and September, up 9 percent from the same period a year earlier. Revenue jumped more than 25 percent over that time, to $140.5 billion in the third quarter.

Aramco credited its performance to the resilience of operations during disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the war in Iran, now in its ninth month, as well as swift recovery work after a series of drone and missile attacks by Iran-backed militants.

The company said the average price of its crude oil was $95 a barrel, 35 percent more than a year ago.

The war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran caused the price of oil to surge and brought an escalating campaign by Houthi fighters, backed by Iran, against Saudi Arabia. Attacks on an international airport in Riyadh claimed more than a dozen lives, while missile strikes have damaged an Aramco headquarters building in the eastern Saudi city of Dhahran, two refineries and an oil processing facility at the Abqaiq oil field.

The attacks have also jeopardized Saudi Arabia’s plans to diversify its economy beyond oil and into one that can derive more growth from tourism, sports and technology. Last month the kingdom postponed its marquee investment conference, known as the Future Investment Initiative. On Tuesday the 2027 Asian Cup, a soccer tournament that was to be hosted in Saudi Arabia on Jan. 7, was postponed for about a year.

Oil prices rose after the U.S. military struck Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, though they pulled back on Tuesday. American officials described the strikes as limited, though President Trump has said he was considering an attack on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections if a diplomatic deal was not reached.

“Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026,” Amin Nasser, the chief executive of Aramco, said in a statement, calling the past months an “extraordinary period.”

Perhaps the most severe attack occurred in September when drones hit Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which stretches about 750 miles from its oil-producing Eastern Province to Yanbu, an export terminal on the Red Sea.

The pipeline is considered a lifeline because it allows the kingdom to export millions of barrels of oil a day while avoiding the Strait of Hormuz.

The attack raised fears that millions of barrels of crude would be stuck inside Saudi Arabia but the pipeline was back online in less than a week. A few weeks later about six million barrels of oil a day were moving through the pipeline. Saudi Arabia said it planned to expand its capacity to as much as 10 million barrels a day within two to three years.

Saudi Arabia has also used tankers navigating the Strait of Hormuz to maintain its crude exports.

On Tuesday Mr. Nasser said the company exported an additional 1.1 million barrels of crude in the third quarter of the year compared with the prior three months, despite the attack on the pipeline.

Work on expanding the East-West pipeline capacity “has already started,” Mr. Nasser said on a call with investors — and added that Saudi Arabia was exploring “additional routes” for getting crude out of the country.

In addition to exporting oil through the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, Saudi Arabia has exported oil through a pipeline to the Mediterranean Sea near the Suez Canal. The Suez route, on the north side of the Red Sea, has helped the kingdom avoid attacks by Houthi militants, but the journey to markets in Asia is far longer and more expensive.

“We’re looking at additional routes, we’re doing the engineering at this stage,” Mr. Nasser said, but he did not offer details on where new bypasses might be.

Aramco’s results add to a wave of eye-popping earnings across the oil industry as the war with Iran causes crude prices to soar — and prices to rise at the pump for consumers.

In the United States, energy companies have earned more than $130 billion in profits since the start of the war, The New York Times found, based on the performance of more than 50 large U.S. oil and gas companies.

item.title: Flouting Consumer Law, Insurers Refuse to Pay Medical Bills for Emergency Care
item.description:
Over the past two years, Flight for Life has airlifted car crash victims, premature babies and adults struggling to breathe to hospitals across southeastern Wisconsin.

Anthem, the major health insurer, covered dozens of those patients, but it has refused to pay $2.1 million it owes the company for their helicopter rides.

The amounts due for each emergency medical flight range from $9,382 to $62,373. Anthem has historically paid its bills, but late last year it suddenly stopped.

“It was like a faucet they just shut off,” said Flight for Life’s executive director, Leif Erickson.

The insurer’s willful nonpayment is the latest in a cascade of unintended consequences brought about by a widely supported law that was intended to protect patients from surprise medical bills.

The law, which took effect in 2022, calls for arbitrators to decide appropriate levels of reimbursement, and it has already triggered millions of disputes between medical care providers and insurers. Doctors have prevailed overwhelmingly, winning arbitration settlements that sometimes far exceeded the usual insurer rates.

Now, fed up with what they consider unfair outcomes, insurers are fighting back by refusing to pay.

The law, the No Surprises Act, was enacted with a large bipartisan majority to ensure patients never got excessive bills in situations, like emergencies, where they could not pick their doctors.

The arbitration system set up by the law was supposed to resolve billing disputes when health care providers and insurers could not agree on a price: An arbitrator reviews a proposed dollar amount from each side and decides which one is most reasonable. Insurers are required to pay that amount within 30 days, and billing patients for anything beyond that is prohibited.

Lawmakers expected the system to be used rarely and to produce reasonable payments. Instead, doctors and other health care providers have been swamping arbitrators with millions of claims, often for amounts that far exceed what is customarily paid for a service. And they have won the vast majority of their cases — sometimes receiving sums such as $440,000 for a breast reduction, $73,000 for an ankle X-ray, or $125,000 for assisting on prostate surgery.

Insurers have sued doctors and lobbied Congress to change the law, contending that the large awards and lopsided results are driving up health insurance premiums.

But with Washington moving slowly, they have adopted the strategy of simply declining to pay.

Nearly 30 percent of arbitration awards has gone unpaid since 2024, according to an analysis of 400,000 such awards provided by a major medical billing firm that The New York Times reviewed.

Anthem’s nonpayment rate was the highest by far, at 74 percent, but other large insurers, including Cigna, UnitedHealthcare and Aetna, have also declined to pay a significant portion.

Share of cases where the insurer did not pay the arbitration award, according to data from HaloMD, a medical billing firm

Note: Analysis of 409,102 cases from January 2024 to July 2026. Only includes cases in which payments to doctors could be reliably tracked.

Source: HaloMD.

By The New York Times

The standoff has created dysfunction and lawlessness in a system that a growing number of lawmakers and administration officials say needs to be changed.

“The providers are succeeding in what feel like egregious award levels, and then the insurers are also doing some of this egregious behavior by not paying,” said Katie Keith, the director of Georgetown University’s Center for Health Policy and the Law. “But there’s not accountability on either side.”

Health plans, including Anthem, criticize HaloMD, the company that provided The Times with payment data, for using business tactics that exploit the arbitration system and result in large payouts. Only one of the major insurers The Times contacted disputed the accuracy of the data. A Cigna spokeswoman said that a significantly smaller share went unpaid in 2026 than what the Halo data showed.

Most large health insurers told The Times it is their policy not to pay awards if they believe the claim should never have qualified for the arbitration process, even when the arbitrator determined it to be eligible.

In the case of Flight for Life, Anthem says it will not pay because it believes the medevac service violated the arbitration system’s complex procedural rules, an assessment Flight for Life disputes.

Ariel Bayewitz, vice president of health economics at Elevance Health, Anthem’s parent company, said that the company “believes strongly” in paying eligible awards on time. But, he said, Anthem estimates that most claims that have moved through the arbitration system should have been found ineligible, because they either didn’t follow the rules or were for situations not covered under the consumer protection law.

“More providers are submitting ineligible cases because ineligible cases aren’t being dismissed like they should be,” he said.

Smaller health plans also have been withholding payments in cases where they think the award is unreasonable. Some even have form letters they send to doctors whose awards they won’t pay.

“The determination is not merely high; it is legally defective,” says one such letter, from the New York insurer EmblemHealth, declining to pay an award 99 times its usual rate for a breast reconstruction.

“Recently, we have observed a significant increase in very high-dollar claims, which we are actively reviewing and challenging as appropriate,” said Alex Gomez, a spokesman for the plan.

A spokeswoman for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which oversees the arbitration system, said the law always requires insurers to pay arbitration awards.

Doctors and air ambulance companies have turned to the courts, filing hundreds of lawsuits to enforce the arbitrators’ decisions, but three federal appeals courts have ruled that the No Surprises Act does not include a right to sue.

Stephen Ware, a professor of law at the University of Kansas, said that unlike most arbitration situations, the No Surprises Act does not explain how a ruling can be enforced. One appeals court decision suggested that the government could sue to force insurers to pay. So far, the Trump administration has not exercised such power.

Doctors have said that the nonpayments make it hard to manage their practices. Some who have built their businesses around the arbitration system and its high payouts have taken on debts to stay afloat.

Dr. Jennifer Raley, a managing partner at Wake Emergency Physicians in North Carolina, said her practice had $1.2 million in outstanding awards. It won 1,032 arbitration cases in 2025, with an average award around four times what insurers typically pay.

In January, it had to take out a line of credit to make payroll.

“We just want to get paid what we need to pay the people who saw the patients,” she said. PHI, a national air ambulance company, recently closed a base in Red Bluff, Calif., a small city between Sacramento and the Oregon border.

In an interview, PHI’s chief executive, Scott McCarty, cited $16.3 million in outstanding payments from Anthem as the cause of the closure.

“The insurance companies cannot unilaterally decide to breach a federal law if they don’t like the end result,” Mr. McCarty said. “That’s essentially what they are doing.”

Anthem spokeswoman Janey Kiryluik said that the insurer was “actively trying to bring PHI Air Medical into our network,” but that the medevac company had requested unreasonably high rates. She said that, in arbitration, it typically requests $56,000 per flight.

Dr. Brian McHugh, a neurosurgeon from Long Island, N.Y., has repeatedly received letters from Anthem challenging his awards on the grounds they are too expensive. Dr. McHugh often wins arbitration awards that are 40 times higher than what Anthem typically pays, according to federal data.

He said other doctors at his practice had stopped seeing Anthem patients.

Ms. Kiryluik said the insurer does not use a financial threshold as a “basis for holding payment,” and that it no longer uses the letter Dr. McHugh received.

Anthem, like all major insurers, supported the No Surprises Act when Congress was writing the legislation during the first Trump administration. But over the last six years, the company’s executives have soured on the law’s arbitration system, saying that it encourages abusive billing. Many of the high awards have been for scheduled procedures, not the emergency care the law was written to address.

Anthem defends its nonpayment policies as intentional. In a 13-page report, it estimated that 60 percent of its cases that arbitrators had decided should never have qualified. This year, it has not paid 83 percent of arbitration claims, according to the HaloMD data, a substantial jump from previous years.

The Labor Department, which oversees large employer health plans, is investigating Anthem’s failure to pay arbitration awards, according to documents The Times obtained. Ms. Kiryluik, the Anthem spokeswoman, said the plan was cooperating with the investigation.

The 400,000 claims that HaloMD shared with The Times make up around two-thirds of the total arbitration cases it has won since 2024. The data set only includes cases for which HaloMD could reliably track payments to doctors.

Anthem and other insurers contend that HaloMD is part of the problem. They say Halo typically submits unreasonably high bids to arbitration, sometimes winning 113 times typical insurer payments. The company has also been accused of filing a high volume of ineligible claims. Five insurers have sued Halo, accusing it of fraudulent behavior. Three of them, including one from Anthem, have been dismissed in federal court, on the grounds that courts can’t review the arbitrators’ decisions.

HaloMD spokesman Patrick Velliky said that the insurers’ lawsuits were “an attempt to intimidate physicians and clinicians out of seeking fair and sustainable reimbursement.”

The law set up a series of deadlines and procedures that doctors need to follow. They limited access to the system to certain situations. Cases where the patient has a government plan, like Medicare or Medicaid, are not eligible. Nor are situations where the doctor already has a contract with the health plan.

Insurers say they sometimes see doctors winning two times for the same care — first in a state-level system to resolve medical billing disputes, and then again through federal arbitration.

“We’re not going to pay it twice,” said Josh Goldberg, executive director of heath policy at Health Care Service Corporation, which covers 27 million people through six Blue Cross affiliates. “This is just a situation where we’re a little bit between a rock and a hard place.”

The insurer is “not the final decider,” said Ms. Keith. She described Anthem’s strategy as “high-risk” because it flouts binding arbitration decisions.

But insurers expressed frustration that the system incentivizes arbitrators to find claims eligible. They get paid a flat fee for each dispute they resolve. If they rule a case is ineligible, they earn nothing.

The No Surprises Act gives the Trump administration authority to fine health insurers $100 for each day they do not pay an arbitration award. So far, it has not issued a single penalty.

Doctors have submitted hundreds of complaints about unpaid awards to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which oversee the system. Those that The Times spoke with said they had rarely received a response.

“There has to be some enforcement,” said Thomas LaGreca, a partner at Callagy Law, which files claims for providers. He estimates that 27 percent of clients claims remain unpaid six months after arbitration decisions. Health plans also said that C.M.S. had failed to respond to thousands of complaints about the large number of ineligible claims.

Spokespeople for both C.M.S. and the Labor Department declined to respond to questions about why they had not issued penalties to enforce the No Surprises Act.

A Trump administration spokesman told The Times in July that “the system is being gamed” by doctors and that the government was “actively working to clean it up.” The administration has not yet announced any policy changes.

Congress has recently taken a greater interest in reform, with one Senate committee hosting round table meetings and a top House Democrat introducing new legislation.

“There are problems on both sides, and I’ll readily admit that,” Representative Greg Murphy, Republican of North Carolina, said in an interview.

But Mr. Murphy, who worked as a urologist before running for office, said he believed that the “majority of abuses” had been committed by insurers who do not pay awards. He has introduced legislation that would stiffen penalties for nonpayment.

“I ran a small business,” he said. “If I don’t have income, guess what happens to the business? It dies.”

Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, chairs the Senate Health Committee and was an architect of the No Surprises Act. He has told those involved in the process that he views fixing its problems before he leaves office in January as a legacy project.

Representative Frank Pallone Jr., Democrat of New Jersey, was also an author of the original law. He has a different idea: abolishing the complex arbitration system altogether. Last month, he introduced a bill that would resolve billing disputes by setting a flat payment for doctors at the level insurers typically pay.

Mr. Pallone has been skeptical of arbitration supporting it as part of a compromise to get the surprise billing ban passed. He said the reality was even more chaotic than he had predicted. “We have the proof with the facts that shows that this arbitration system is out of hand,” he said.

item.title: She’s Fighting to Cover Iowa Politics, One Closed Door at a Time
item.description:
The smirk stuck with Laura Belin, a left-leaning journalist who covers Iowa politics.

A press aide to Gov. Kim Reynolds, a Republican, flashed it at her as he shut her out of a January budget briefing, just moments after welcoming in a scrum of other reporters.

“This is a private office,” he said, closing the door in her face. Ms. Belin said he seemed “very happy” as he did so.

For two decades, Ms. Belin has been publishing investigative journalism and political analysis on her site, Bleeding Heartland, as well as a more recent Substack account, powered by records requests, inside sources, open meetings and public information. She also co-hosts a radio show on KHOI, based in Ames, Iowa. The Washington Post, The Des Moines Cityview, Politico, Esquire and Talking Points Memo have cited Ms. Belin’s reporting.

Her beat is hot right now: Iowa is bursting with competitive elections, including the neck-and-neck U.S. Senate race between Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican, and Josh Turek, a Democratic state representative.

A longtime Democrat, Ms. Belin is unabashedly liberal in her work. Her write-ups have the feel of something that MS NOW or HuffPost, two left-leaning national outlets, might publish.

She also donates to the Democratic politicians she covers — something many traditional journalism outlets, including The New York Times, NPR, Politico and The Associated Press, strongly discourage or explicitly forbid. Fox News allows its journalists to donate to campaigns; MS NOW and The Huffington Post do not.

Her open embrace of one party appears to have resulted in quite a few doors closed by the other. Her requests for credentials to cover the Iowa House triggered denial after denial; her requests to sit among her peers years ago on the Iowa Senate’s media row met with a similar fate, until authorities booted all reporters from the space. Her attempts to get patched in to Senator Charles Grassley’s news conference calls have ended in frustration; and she has even struggled to get on press distribution lists.

At the same time, Ms. Belin isn’t partisan enough to qualify for the red carpet treatment that campaigns around the country are increasingly rolling out for internet influencers, bypassing traditional journalists in favor of friendlier interviews. Three times in this election cycle, Ms. Belin said, she has attended events for Democratic candidates at which influencers got one-on-one interviews with top candidates while reporters were left to ask their questions in a group setting.

It’s a modest slight in comparison with what Ms. Belin faces from the other side of the aisle. But her ongoing fight for press access highlights the shifting definition of what it means to be a reporter in a fractured and increasingly opinionated media landscape. Podcasters and Substack writers with clear biases are finding larger and larger audiences, even as the institutions they cover demand objectivity and neutrality.

The Republican Party of Iowa didn’t respond to a question about Ms. Belin’s struggle for access, though a spokeswoman pointed to her history of donating to politicians she covers and her statement that she does not “pretend to be objective” or hide her opinions.

Waiting for enough results

Initial votes have been reported. Once we see enough data, we’ll turn on our real-time estimates of who will win the Senate and the House.

Waiting for estimates

Waiting for estimates

Ms. Belin points out that her donations are a matter of public record and that she also writes skeptical pieces about Democrats and their prospects in Iowa.

“I’m writing the stories that I would want to read and covering the news in the way that I want to cover it,” she said.

Access makes a “real difference,” she said. “And I think that if it didn’t, I don’t think they would have gone to such lengths to exclude me from all these opportunities.”

Diving into Iowa politics wasn’t Ms. Belin’s initial plan. After graduating from Harvard University in 1991, she got a master’s in Russian studies from the University of Oxford and proceeded to cover Russian politics for a Prague-based research institute and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

But Ms. Belin’s interest in state politics won the professional tug of war against Vladimir V. Putin’s use of state power. When Bleeding Heartland launched in 2007, Ms. Belin, who grew up in Iowa, first joined as a frequent commenter under the handle “desmoinesdem.” The site’s management was impressed enough with her feedback to ask her to write articles.

She was off and posting. “I had a toddler and a preschooler,” recalled Ms. Belin, who eventually took over the site. “I was like, ‘Oh, yeah, I could do this — this is fine.’”

Ms. Belin has built an audience via ubiquity, toting her video tripod from event to event and chasing down politicians for quotes. Like many independent journalists, Ms. Belin keeps her sites fresh with analysis and commentary from herself and others, but she pursues investigative projects as well, like a story about how Governor Reynolds used Covid relief funds to pay staff in her office. Though the governor denied inappropriate spending, a state audit later found fault with her actions. The U.S. Treasury Department earlier this year disputed the findings of the state audit.

“No one else was interested in the governor’s office budget,” noted Ms. Belin via email.

“She does excellent original reporting, she’s meticulous in her research, she’s ethical and she’s accurate,” said Kathie Obradovich, editor in chief of The Iowa Capital Dispatch, an affiliate of the nonprofit States Newsroom.

Ms. Belin’s family home in the Des Moines suburbs, which she inherited, serves as the home base for Bleeding Heartland, as well as the stomping ground for Sammy, a mixed-breed dog who sets up shop on a well-worn pet bed alongside Ms. Belin’s workstation once he ascertains that all is quiet.

The troubles for Ms. Belin start when she ventures from her cozy, solo newsroom. Starting in 2019, Ms. Belin was repeatedly denied a press pass to cover the Iowa House, which has long been under Republican control. The initial rationale for withholding credentials was that they are “not issued to members of the public.” A year later, she was told that credentials are not issued to outlets that are “nontraditional/independent in nature.”

After about five years of back and forth, Ms. Belin sued for access in a federal court. Days later, the Iowa House granted Ms. Belin the credentials.

The Iowa Senate in 2022 took a more dramatic step. Rather than tussle with Ms. Belin and other independent reporters, it booted all the journalists from the media row at the front of the chamber and relocated them to the nosebleed seats high above the action on the floor. A spokesman blamed “nontraditional” outlets for creating problems.

She also claims that she has been excluded from the conference calls that Senator Grassley holds for reporters. Mr. Grassley’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

Republicans don’t hold a monopoly on Ms. Belin’s hassles over access. At the Iowa Democratic Party’s convention in June, for example, progressive influencers were granted individual interviews with the party’s top hopefuls. Ms. Belin and other reporters took part in a short group interview with Rob Sand, the Democratic candidate for governor.

When Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky came to Des Moines, also in June, to barnstorm with Mr. Sand, influencers were accorded privileged access for a video highlighting the event. Ms. Belin and others struggled to land their questions in a loud group interview with the politicians.

So Ms. Belin will continue showing up wherever she can get a seat. In June, she videotaped the public meeting of a state panel on the ballot eligibility of some Libertarian candidates — a recording that a state court later relied on for key findings, calling it “high quality.”

And on a Wednesday evening in mid-October, Ms. Belin went to the headquarters of Iowa PBS for a debate between Chris McGowan, a Republican, and Dave Dawson, a Democrat, in the race to represent Iowa’s Fourth Congressional District. She wanted to buttonhole the candidates after the event, especially Mr. McGowan.

Once the polemics concluded, Ms. Belin hustled to the lobby and conducted an interview with Mr. Dawson. She later learned that Mr. McGowan had left the building, somehow bypassing her.

“I had so many questions for him!” said Ms. Belin.

Sheelagh McNeill and Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: The Soaring Cost of Diesel Is Bankrupting Small Trucking Companies
item.description:
Once a week for a year, Luis Escalante spread envelopes across his kitchen table, sorting them into piles of past-due bills. Between costly repairs on his semi trucks and increased competition, he was struggling to keep his small Southern California trucking company profitable.

Then the war in Iran started. Diesel prices in the state jumped well over $5 a gallon. Then $6 and $7. Paying thousands of dollars more for fuel every month, Mr. Escalante, 47, could no longer afford the high-interest loans buoying his business, and he reluctantly accepted the last-ditch plan he had long dreaded: filing for bankruptcy.

“I had to be honest with myself,” he said. “There was no way to keep going.”

Almost all industries have faced downstream impacts from the war, but the high price of diesel has been particularly hard for farmers, who use it to power machinery, and truckers, who are paying around 70 percent more per gallon than they were a year ago. In September, at least 40 trucking companies nationwide, including Mr. Escalante’s, filed for bankruptcy, according to BKwire, a bankruptcy data analytics firm. It was a 38 percent increase from a year earlier.

While every failing business has its own story, logistics experts and bankruptcy lawyers say record-breaking diesel prices have been a contributing factor, especially for small operators.

“When diesel goes from under $4 a gallon to over $6 in a year and freight rates don’t follow, the difference comes straight out of the owner’s pocket,” said David Cruz, a bankruptcy lawyer in Florida. He has seen an uptick in trucking companies contacting his office since the war began, he added.

Last month, President Trump, who authorized the U.S.-Israeli attack that started the war in February, signed an executive order allowing anyone to buy so-called red-dyed diesel, which is typically restricted to off-road uses like farm operations, and deferring and possibly eliminating some taxes on the fuel.

“This targeted action,” the order said, “will put money directly in the pocket of American farmers, truckers and workers.”

But for many truckers, the relief isn’t enough.

Rising fuel prices “are essentially a final nail in the coffin” for many small operators, said Desiree Wood, a former trucker and president of the trade group Real Women in Trucking. That segment of the industry grew rapidly during the high-demand days early in the Covid pandemic but has become oversaturated in the years since.

As a boy in Tijuana, Mexico, Mr. Escalante, watched the long lines of semi trucks waiting to cross into the United States and imagined the drivers heading to far-flung destinations. Maybe San Francisco, Chicago, even New York. Places he had seen only in movies. One day, he told himself, he would be the one behind the wheel.

When he moved to Southern California in his 20s, he studied for his commercial driver’s license and found work hauling fast-food utensils to Burger King and Chick-fil-A locations across the country. He eventually drove to all those cities he had thought about as a boy.

But the grueling cross-country travel kept Mr. Escalante away from his wife and young children in Riverside County, so around 2016 he and a friend started a small trucking company. They named it A&B Transportation, liking the simplicity and the ring of the first letters of the alphabet.

“Who doesn’t want to be their own boss?” Mr. Escalante said, recalling those early years. “I had always worked for other people. Now this was my version of a dream coming true.”

The company grew slowly but consistently, eventually owning eight trucks and employing eight drivers. The lockdowns of 2020 ushered in a heyday for truckers. Consumers holed up at home with stimulus checks were suddenly buying new furniture, laptops, cars, personal protective equipment, walking shoes. To match the demand, trucking companies were hiring, and some drivers ventured out on their own. A round trip between Southern California and Texas could pay $8,000 before expenses, Mr. Escalante said.

“It was the busiest and best time to be a trucker,” he said.

He quickly paid off a $100,000 loan he had taken out to cover maintenance on his aging fleet, and his business was comfortably profitable. But when the pandemic rush slowed, A&B Transportation faced a slate of new competitors that often offered to move freight at bargain rates to entice customers.

It grew harder to find loads for his drivers, Mr. Escalante said, and that same Texas round trip brought in only $2,600. He couldn’t keep up with payroll and, in a panicked move that he acknowledges wasn’t a wise business decision, took out around $200,000 in loans. He used the money to replace some of his aging trailers and pay drivers.

By the end of 2024, A&B, unable to pay what it had in the past, lost most of its drivers. Mr. Escalante and his co-founder were the only drivers, and they had to sell some of the fleet.

“I kept thinking, ‘This will get better,’” even as he stopped making payments on his loans, Mr. Escalante said.

Big players like Walmart and Amazon, which have their own fleets, can withstand higher diesel costs. So can large trucking companies, which use long-term contracts with fuel surcharges that allow them to pass higher diesel prices on to customers, said Erich Muehlegger, an economics professor at the University of California, Davis, who studies transportation markets.

But small, for-hire companies like Mr. Escalante’s are far less insulated, and last year they made up around 90 percent of 580,000 active trucking companies, according to an analysis of federal data by the American Trucking Associations.

Mr. Cruz, the Florida lawyer, represents a trucking company that delivers cargo for Amazon and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September. He has seen smaller companies get caught in a trap, he said: Lenders would repossess their trucks when they fell two or three payments behind, which stripped them of any way to earn the money to catch up on payments. Filing for bankruptcy, he noted, triggers an automatic stay, which stops repossession.

“Diesel is a cost the whole economy pays, but small carriers pay it first,” Mr. Cruz said, “and they pay it with their trucks.”

That was the case for A&B Transportation, which lost three trucks to repossession after failing to make payments, Mr. Escalante said. Still, he tried to hold on.

He carefully planned his routes to minimize filling up in California, where taxes make fuel more costly, instead favoring a Pilot station along Interstate 10 just past the state line in Arizona. But even there, prices hovered close to $6 a gallon. It cost him around $900 to fill up his 150-gallon tank — more than a third of what he made on the entire trip to and from Texas.

When Mr. Escalante got tired of listening to old-school hip-hop songs on the road, he flipped to talk radio, where he heard about the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and how it would keep raising fuel prices worldwide. Officials, including Mr. Trump, kept saying the pain at the pump would be temporary. But interest kept accruing, and his loans went to collections.

Mr. Escalante felt overwhelmed by stress. His shame over the idea of filing for bankruptcy was replaced by a sense that it was the least bad option.

In April, he and his wife, Claudia, sat down at the kitchen table again. He stumbled over his words as he explained that a Chapter 7 liquidation seemed like their best alternative.

It would mean closing the business, his credit score would take a big hit and he’d need time to save up for a bankruptcy lawyer, but there was no feasible way to repay the company’s more than $500,000 in liabilities, which far exceeded its assets of less than $50,000.

“I’ll be able to start over and rebuild,” Mr. Escalante told his wife. She cried and told him that she wanted whatever was best for their future.

Mr. Escalante took a job as a driver for another small company and these days hauls loads as far as the Upper Midwest and earns close to 65 cents per mile.

On Sept. 11, AAA logged a diesel price that was at the time the highest national average ever recorded — $6.05 a gallon. That same day, Mr. Escalante signed the paperwork sending A&B Transportation into bankruptcy.

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: How TV Networks Plan to Cover the Midterm Elections
item.description:
Inflation may be a top concern for voters in Tuesday’s midterm elections — but broadcast TV is embracing it.

As recently as 2014, the Big Three networks — ABC, CBS and NBC — aired little more than an hour or two of live coverage of midterm results, barely a blip between reality shows, sitcoms and procedurals.

On Tuesday, NBC will offer its local stations 13 consecutive hours of nonstop coverage, beginning in the late afternoon and extending all the way through early Wednesday. CBS and ABC will hand over their entire prime-time coverage to election results, and will return for more coverage overnight.

Because the results span hundreds of local races, midterm nights do not always offer the same tidy on-air narrative that a presidential election promises. But with the balance of power in Congress at stake — and Democrats and Republicans alike calling the evening existential — executives are expecting significant audience interest in Tuesday’s returns.

Here is a look at how the broadcast and cable networks, as well as some of the newer digital outlets, are covering the results.

Waiting for enough results

Initial votes have been reported. Once we see enough data, we’ll turn on our real-time estimates of who will win the Senate and the House.

Waiting for estimates

Waiting for estimates

NBC will start coverage at 5 p.m. Eastern, and won’t stop until 6 a.m. Wednesday. (Local affiliates will have the opportunity to take the entire package, or to take breaks for their local newscasts.)

The network’s coverage will be helmed by the “Today” anchor Savannah Guthrie, the “Nightly News” anchor Tom Llamas, the “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker and the correspondent Hallie Jackson. The popular data-cruncher Steve Kornacki will return to his usual perch, ready to frantically punch at his big board. The “Kornacki Cam,” a continuous livestream of the NBC data analyst, will go live at 5:30 p.m.

CBS formally kicks off coverage at 7 p.m., led by the “Evening News” anchor Tony Dokoupil, the morning show co-hosts Gayle King and Norah O’Donnell, and the “Face the Nation” moderator Margaret Brennan. A livestreamed “Nerd Show” featuring the network’s polling experts will simultaneously air online from 5 p.m. to 2 a.m.

And ABC will kick off four consecutive hours of coverage at 7 p.m., with the “World News Tonight” anchor David Muir leading the coverage. Mr. Muir, along with a team that includes “World News Tonight” Sunday anchor Linsey Davis and “This Week” co-anchor Martha Raddatz, will be live for seven consecutive hours on ABC News Live, Hulu and Disney+.

Fox News’s coverage will be hosted by the anchors Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum, with Bill Hemmer utilizing the interactive digital map known as “The Bill Board.” An A.I. chatbot has been created on the channel’s app so users can ask specific questions about ongoing results. And Arnon Mishkin, the cello-playing pollster, will again be in charge of the network’s decision desk.

Jake Tapper and Anderson Cooper will lead CNN’s coverage, which includes John King and his usual “magic wall,” the name of his touch screen interactive map. The network said Mr. King would be outfitted with multiple magic walls for the first time, featuring additional data. On MS NOW, Rachel Maddow will lead an ensemble team including network favorites like Nicolle Wallace and Ari Melber. The anchor Ali Velshi is in charge of the “Big Board,” its digital interactive map.

Of course, there will be hundreds of online sources for voters to consult, too. Nate Silver, the veteran election forecaster, will host a livestream with, among others, the writer Matt Yglesias. The Dispatch will host another livestream that begins at 9 p.m. Eastern. Chuck Todd and Chris Cillizza are collaborating with Decision Desk HQ, a polling and results-counting service, for livestreamed coverage. (The NewsNation cable network will also be using data from Decision Desk for its five-hour special beginning at 7 p.m.) The Free Press will also have a livestream with Mark Halperin’s video platform, “2WAY.”

There will be, however, few late-night shows offering an on-the-fly comedic take on the results. CBS’s “Late Show” with Stephen Colbert, which regularly aired live episodes on major election nights, was canceled this year. NBC’s extensive coverage means there will be no reactions from Seth Meyers or Jimmy Fallon. “The Daily Show” has a new episode (with Ronny Chieng hosting), but it is taping in the late afternoon.

ABC’s “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” will air a new episode in its usual slot at 11:35 p.m., but it will not be live. Still, there could be some news. “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” is taping later than usual — after 9 p.m. Eastern — so it can incorporate some early results, and Mr. Kimmel’s guests will be the progressive hosts from the “Pod Save America” podcast.
